"**Zombie**" is a [protest song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_song "Protest song") by Irish [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") band [the Cranberries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cranberries "The Cranberries"). It was written by the lead singer, [Dolores O'Riordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_O'Riordan "Dolores O'Riordan"), about the young victims of a [bombing in Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_bombings "Warrington bombings"), England, during [the Troubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles "The Troubles") in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland"). The song was released on 19 September 1994 by [Island Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Records "Island Records") as the [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single") from the Cranberries' second studio album, *[No Need to Argue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Need_to_Argue "No Need to Argue")* (1994). Critics have described "Zombie" as "a masterpiece of alternative rock", with [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge")\-style distorted guitar and shouted vocals uncharacteristic of the band's other work.

While Island Records feared releasing a politically charged song as a single, "Zombie" reached No. 1 on the charts of Australia, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, and Iceland. The song was ineligible for the US *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* [Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_100 "Hot 100") chart, but it reached No. 1 on the US *Billboard* [Alternative Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_Songs "Alternative Songs") chart. Listeners of the Australian radio station [Triple J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J "Triple J") voted it No. 1 on the [1994 Triple J Hottest 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J_Hottest_100,_1994 "Triple J Hottest 100, 1994") chart, and it won the Best Song Award at the [1995 MTV Europe Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MTV_Europe_Music_Awards "1995 MTV Europe Music Awards"). The music video was directed by [Samuel Bayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Bayer "Samuel Bayer"), and featured O'Riordan singing while painted gold, and footage of war-torn Belfast. In April 2020, it became the first song by an Irish group to surpass one billion views on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube").

The Cranberries noted that "Zombie" drew strong responses from audiences. After O'Riordan's death in 2018, it became an Irish [stadium anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium_anthem "Stadium anthem"), first for the teams from the Cranberries' hometown of [Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limerick "Limerick"), and later for the [Ireland national rugby union team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_national_rugby_union_team "Ireland national rugby union team") starting in the [2023 Rugby World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Rugby_World_Cup "2023 Rugby World Cup"). The band recorded acoustic, stripped-down versions on *[MTV Unplugged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Unplugged "MTV Unplugged")* and the 2017 album *[Something Else](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Something_Else_\(The_Cranberries_album\) "Something Else (The Cranberries album)")*. "Zombie" has been covered by numerous artists; O'Riordan had planned to contribute vocals to a version by the American band [Bad Wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Wolves "Bad Wolves"), which was released days after her death.

## Background and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and composition")\]

[The Troubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles "The Troubles") were a conflict in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") from the late 1960s to 1998\.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) The [Provisional Irish Republican Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army "Provisional Irish Republican Army") (IRA), an [Irish republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_republican "Irish republican") paramilitary organisation, waged an [armed campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army_campaign "Provisional Irish Republican Army campaign") to end British rule in Northern Ireland and [unite the region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Ireland "United Ireland") with the [Republic of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland"). Republican and [Loyalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_loyalism "Ulster loyalism") paramilitaries killed more than 3,500 people, many from [thousands of bomb attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bombings_during_the_Troubles "List of bombings during the Troubles").[\[4\]](#cite_note-Taulbee-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) One of the bombings happened on 20 March 1993, as two IRA [improvised explosive devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvised_explosive_device "Improvised explosive device") hidden in litter bins [were detonated in a shopping street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_bombings "Warrington bombings") in [Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington "Warrington"), England. Two children were killed in the attack: Johnathan Ball, aged 3, and Tim Parry, aged 12\. 56 people were injured.[\[6\]](#cite_note-UPI-1993-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Ball died at the scene of the bombing as a result of his fragmentation-inflicted injuries, and five days later, Parry died in a hospital as a result of head injuries.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) O'Riordan decided to write a song that reflected upon the event and the children's deaths after visiting the town:[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10)

> There were a lot of bombs going off in London and I remember this one time a child was killed when a bomb was put in a rubbish bin – that's why there's that line in the song, 'A child is slowly taken'. \[ ... \] We were on a tour bus and I was near the location where it happened, so it really struck me hard – I was quite young, but I remember being devastated about the innocent children being pulled into that kind of thing. So I suppose that's why I was saying, 'It's not me' – that even though I'm Irish it wasn't me, I didn't do it. Because being Irish, it was quite hard, especially in the UK when there was so much tension.

— Dolores O'Riordan in 2017, on writing "Zombie".[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10)

O'Riordan said "Zombie" came to her "subconsciously" midway through the Cranberries' English tour in 1993,[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) writing the core chords on her acoustic guitar.[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10) Once O'Riordan was back in her hometown of [Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limerick "Limerick") and returned to her flat after a night out,[\[12\]](#cite_note-LS-Johnston2017-12)[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10) she played those chords and started building a song around them, quickly "coming up with the chorus, which was catchy and anthemic",[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) and soon moving onto the verses.[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10) O'Riordan took the song idea, originally titled "In Your Head", into the Cranberries' small rehearsal shed in [Mungret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mungret "Mungret").[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14) Given she was playing an acoustic guitar, the rest of the band initially followed along in, as guitarist [Noel Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Hogan "Noel Hogan") put it, "that kind of sweet [indie pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_pop "Indie pop") thing" that the band featured in their other songs, before O'Riordan decided that it was not what she wanted,[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15) picked up an electric guitar and stated that "it needs to be heavy because it's angry". Drummer Fergal Lawler recalled that usually in that small room, "you're trying to keep it low because you don't want to deafen anybody", but O'Riordan played it loud and "we couldn't really hear the lyrics because she was singing through her guitar", and that the singer was adamant that she wanted more [distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distortion_\(music\) "Distortion (music)") pedals on the guitars and asked for more strength than usual in drumming.[\[16\]](#cite_note-UDM-Lawler20200919-16)[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14)

## Production and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Production and release")\]

> "Years from now, when alternative rock is just a distant memory from a time long forgotten, certain songs will remain. 'Zombie' will forever live on as a true classic moment from a truly classic era of music. Not before or since has a band hit on a moment and absolutely capitalised like The Cranberries did with 'Zombie'. ... Thank you for giving us alternative rock's true masterpiece".

— Author Joe Hughes, in 2018\.[\[17\]](#cite_note-AN-Hughes2018-17)

Soon after "Zombie" was completed, the Cranberries added it to their set list. Lawler said they performed it for a year before recording it, and audiences responded with enthusiasm.[\[18\]](#cite_note-RS-Blistein2019-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) The song was recorded and mixed at [the Manor Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Manor_Studio "The Manor Studio") in Oxford\] and at [Townhouse Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townhouse_Studios "Townhouse Studios") in London in 1994 with producer [Stephen Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Street "Stephen Street").[\[20\]](#cite_note-studios-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-CDbooklet-21) They spent a long time working on getting the [guitar settings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_tunings "Guitar tunings") right to give a suitably expansive sound, with O'Riordan noting "the sound came organically, because we were using our live instruments, we were plugging in a lot, and we started to mess around with [feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_feedback "Audio feedback") and distortion".[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) Hogan contributed [rhythm guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_guitar "Rhythm guitar") to provide textures under O'Riordan's [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff").[\[22\]](#cite_note-Fuller2018-01-23-22) "Zombie" departed from the strings and [jangle guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jangle "Jangle") of the Cranberries' debut album, *[Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody_Else_Is_Doing_It,_So_Why_Can't_We%3F "Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?")* (1993).[\[12\]](#cite_note-LS-Johnston2017-12)[\[23\]](#cite_note-RS-Bienstock2018-23) Hogan said it made them realise "that you can actually be heavy and still have melody", marking a change in their composition style and performances.[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15)

Knowing its potential, the Cranberries wanted "Zombie" to be the lead single for their album *[No Need to Argue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Need_to_Argue "No Need to Argue")*.[\[18\]](#cite_note-RS-Blistein2019-18) Their former manager, Allen Kovac, said that [Island Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Records "Island Records") urged them not to release the "politically urgent" song as a single, and that O'Riordan had ripped up a $1-million cheque the label offered her to work on another song.[\[24\]](#cite_note-RS-Browne2018-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOM-2020-01-15-25) "Dolores was a very small, fragile person, but very opinionated," said Kovac. "Her belief was that she was an international artist and she wanted to break the rest of the world, and 'Zombie' was part of that evolution. She felt the need to expand beyond 'I love you, you love me' and write about what was happening in Ireland at the time", he said.[\[24\]](#cite_note-RS-Browne2018-24) Island Records and management also said "Zombie" was "too controversial, you might not get played on the radio".[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) Hogan added that the label were not expecting a lead single sounding different from the band's output "instead of coming out with another '[Linger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linger_\(The_Cranberries_song\) "Linger (The Cranberries song)")' or '[Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreams_\(The_Cranberries_song\) "Dreams (The Cranberries song)")'".[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15) Lawler recalled arguing to the record label that during the year the band had played "Zombie" in concert, "for a new song that the audience hadn't heard before, they really reacted to it",[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) which was "a sign that it's a catchy song. People like it. It has to work.”[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15) Over time, "\[w\]e pushed and pushed and eventually they decided to release it", he said.[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) By the time the single for "Zombie" was released on 19 September 1994,[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) as well as its parent album *No Need to Argue* the following month, with a music video in heavy rotation on [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV"), the Cranberries were catapulted to international stardom.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](#cite_note-NYT-20180116-28) Shortly after, ideological beliefs came rushing to the forefront of local newspapers, criticising O'Riordan for writing about the Troubles.[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14) O'Riordan said she "knew that would be the angle of the song, because it was controversial".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) Assessing the cultural impact of their song, Hogan responded: "Because of this song, people thought we were a political band. ... Far from it. Dolores always wrote from the heart".[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14) O'Riordan would later state, "If I think something, I have to say it. And I really don't care what anybody thinks, you know?".[\[30\]](#cite_note-NPR-Limbong2018-30) *[NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR")*'s Andrew Limbong, speaking after O'Riordan's death in 2018, said "even though it was a political song, it wasn't necessarily politics she was interested in writing about".[\[30\]](#cite_note-NPR-Limbong2018-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-VOX1994-31) O'Riordan said, "I just cannot accept children being slaughtered at the hands of political violence", and hoped that "it might make people reflect a bit on our society and what we've become."[\[32\]](#cite_note-LAT-Bream94-32)

## Music and lyrics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music and lyrics")\]

"Zombie" has been characterised by commentators as [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock")[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) and [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge").[\[35\]](#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](#cite_note-36) O'Riordan later said it was not a concerted effort to ride the grunge movement, but she stated that "this wasn't grunge, but the timing was good", adding that, "We were just a different type of a band... and we had a lot of our own ideas".[\[12\]](#cite_note-LS-Johnston2017-12)[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) Hogan noted in a *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* interview that the Cranberries were beforehand accepted by "the same kind of \[grunge\] audience".[\[23\]](#cite_note-RS-Bienstock2018-23) O'Riordan was responsible for the heavier sound,[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) a mere expression of her musical taste, as she would say later "we got it out of our system... all that anger out of our system".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) Discussing the musical approach and the requirement of a sound significantly louder, Hogan explained in a 2012 interview with [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam")'s *FaceCulture* that "the heavier sound was the right thing for the song. If it was soft, it wouldn't have had that impact. It would stand out in the live set because of that."[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) Particularly offended that [terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army#Categorisation "Provisional Irish Republican Army") claimed to have carried out these acts in the name of Ireland,[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) O'Riordan asserted: "The IRA are not me. I'm not the IRA. The Cranberries are not the IRA. My family are not. When it says in the song, '*It's not me, it's not my family*,' that's what I'm saying. It's not Ireland, it's some idiots living in the past."[\[31\]](#cite_note-VOX1994-31)[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37) O'Riordan received criticism for the "hard-hitting lyrics"; she responded that it was written from a humanitarian perspective.[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) O’Riordan's mother, Eileen, said: "It wasn’t written as a political song but as an anti-violence, an anti-war song."[\[38\]](#cite_note-38)

O'Riordan never revealed the origin of the "zombie" reference in the lyrics, a concept which admits a personal interpretation of its meaning.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) However, there was a divergence of opinion among writers on the subject. Writing for *The Telegraph*, Ed Power formulated his own hypothesis, saying that the word *Zombie* was "a commentary on how blindly cleaving to centuries old prejudices can reduce \[one's\] capacity for independent thought".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) *Culture Trip* writer Graham Fuller commented that the metaphor perhaps "reanimates the children whose deaths inspired O'Riordan to write it".[\[22\]](#cite_note-Fuller2018-01-23-22) Sonia Saraiya, music and TV critic from *[Miami Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Herald "Miami Herald")* and *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")*, had a different view, saying that the *Zombie* is not the dead children, but "the dead children that populate your mind; the dead bodies you've seen in the images that you can't forget".[\[39\]](#cite_note-VARIETY-Saraiya2018-39)

### Singing voice

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Singing voice")\]

O'Riordan's vocals were noted as reminiscent of the [sean-nós singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean-nós_singing "Sean-nós singing") style,[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41)[\[28\]](#cite_note-NYT-20180116-28) for the [rapid and repeated changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato "Vibrato") in [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_\(music\) "Pitch (music)"), most notably [yodeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yodeling "Yodeling")[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41) when she does the sharp break[\[42\]](#cite_note-42) from [chest register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chest_register "Chest register") to [head register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_register "Head register") in the second [syllable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable "Syllable") of the word *Zom-bie*,[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41) and doing an [amplified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_resonation "Vocal resonation") method forming her [vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowels "Vowels") and [consonants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonants "Consonants").[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41) This creates a vocal trademark when combined with the Gaelic [keening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keening "Keening"),[\[43\]](#cite_note-43) the [lilting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilting "Lilting") vocables,[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) and sung in her thick [Irish accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brogue_\(accent\) "Brogue (accent)").[\[45\]](#cite_note-TIME-20180116-45)[\[28\]](#cite_note-NYT-20180116-28) Author [Bart Plantenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bart_Plantenga "Bart Plantenga") wrote in his book *Yodel in Hi-Fi: From Kitsch Folk to Contemporary Electronica* that "\[h\]er waify, quavering, breaking voice has a natural 'Celtic yodel' in it. It can also be heard on 'Zombie'" \[and other songs\] used "for fantastic emotional effect".[\[46\]](#cite_note-46) Mikael Wood of *Los Angeles Times* described O'Riordan "pushing her voice to a jagged extreme to embody the pain", with a "desperate, yodeling vocal that conjures some ancient emotion".[\[47\]](#cite_note-47) *Far Out Magazine* commented that her vocal performance was "guttural, pleading, captivating and utterly unique, O'Riordan begs for humanity the only way she knew how".[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOM-2020-01-15-25) Saraiya wrote that her voice "often seemed bigger than her petite frame", and also commented that the chorus "practically grunted out of her otherwise bell-like voice with a guttural vowel sound".[\[39\]](#cite_note-VARIETY-Saraiya2018-39)

> O'Riordan's voice is just in a league all its own. She makes no effort to hide her accent. In fact, it adds a richness and character to her voice. O'Riordan lays it all out on the table. Beautifully. Uncompromising and unrelenting. O'Riordan sinks her hooks into you and holds you hostage with her breathtaking vocal onslaught.

— Joe Hughes, *How The Cranberries Blew Away Nirvana With Definitive Grunge Song "Zombie"* – *Alternative Nation*.[\[17\]](#cite_note-AN-Hughes2018-17)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

### Praise

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Praise")\]

*Tedium'*s editor, Ernie Smith, said that O'Riordan wrote "Zombie" in a moment of anger and passion, and called it "one of the defining songs of the alternative rock era".[\[48\]](#cite_note-TEDIUM-48) Rebecca Black of the *[Belfast Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast_Telegraph "Belfast Telegraph")* described "Zombie" as an "outraged response to the Warrington bombs",[\[49\]](#cite_note-49) while music reporter Mark Savage wrote that "her pain was real", describing it as "a visceral response to the death of two children".[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37) In a contemporary review, *[Hot Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Press "Hot Press")* praised "Zombie" and its arrangements, saying that it was stylistically different from the band's previous works: "[Staccato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staccato "Staccato") rhythms and subtle jerks and pauses in the music and the singing make this more than just business-as-usual for the Cranberries. A slow, brooding [Siouxsie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siouxsie_Sioux "Siouxsie Sioux")\-like buzzing guitar melody and dirge-like bass and drums counterpoint the elliptical and impassioned vocals of Dolores O'Riordan as she works her way through the internal psychic and external human tragedies of the Troubles \[...\] "Zombie" signals a growth in confidence".[\[50\]](#cite_note-50) *[The Rough Guide to Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_Guides#Music "Rough Guides")* identified the album *No Need to Argue* as "more of the same" as the Cranberries' debut album, except for the song "Zombie", which had an "angry grunge" sound and "aggressive" lyrics.[\[51\]](#cite_note-51) Music critic [Evelyn McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_McDonnell "Evelyn McDonnell") allowed that O'Riordan had a "certain naivety to her and also a real toughness".[\[30\]](#cite_note-NPR-Limbong2018-30) New York arts editor Graham Fuller partially echoed this view, saying "she was right, but that naivety serves a song that's an unfiltered reaction to a tragedy. It goes with Zombie's primal fury; slicker lyrics would have diluted the song's rawness."[\[22\]](#cite_note-Fuller2018-01-23-22)

Music critic [Neil McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_McCormick "Neil McCormick") wrote that it was the Cranberries' "fiercest rock song... An accusatory lament, it grapples with the endless recriminations of the Irish Troubles, with a slow rolling bass line and thumping mid-tempo beat, finding tension between melodic delicacy and introspection in the verses with a keening, wailing chorus charged with distorted grungy guitars".[\[52\]](#cite_note-52) *[Music & Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_&_Media "Music & Media")* stated that it "combines moody soundscapes with some grunge-y guitar attacks that together make an arresting number".[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) Mark Morris from *[Select](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Select_\(magazine\) "Select (magazine)")* wrote in his review of the album, "The surprise is 'Zombie', a [Sinéad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinéad_O'Connor "Sinéad O'Connor")\-like tantrum of crunchy guitars and confused lyrics about guns and bombs."[\[54\]](#cite_note-54) [Charles Aaron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Aaron "Charles Aaron") from *[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_\(magazine\) "Spin (magazine)")* commented, "I like "Zombie" because its crunching, troubled guitar fuzz was the loudest thing on MTV during the last days of '94. Just ask Bono, my Irish Setter. He's still wailing."[\[55\]](#cite_note-55) Josh Jones of Open Culture, described the "[Gen X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_X#Arts_and_culture "Generation X") heyday"'s song, as "O'Riordan's stadium-size hit ... and its beautifully pained laments and pointedly unsubtle yelps and wails—a stunning expression of mourning that reverberates still some 25 years later".[\[56\]](#cite_note-OC-Jones2018-56) Martin Aston of *[Music Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Week "Music Week")* wrote: "Having broken the UK on the back of their US success, the Cranberries continue to use their pop acumen to fashion wonderful, wistful pop nuggets. 'Zombie' is a little heavier and less user-friendly than 'Linger' and 'Dreams', but no less sublime for it."[\[57\]](#cite_note-57) In 2018, *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* and *[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")* ranked it number three and number two, respectively, on their lists of the top ten Cranberries songs.[\[58\]](#cite_note-58)[\[59\]](#cite_note-59)

On 16 January 2018, following O'Riordan's death, [Colin Parry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tim_Parry_Johnathan_Ball_Foundation_for_Peace "The Tim Parry Johnathan Ball Foundation for Peace"), father of IRA victim Tim Parry, thanked O'Riordan for the "both majestic and also very real lyrics".[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37) "Many people have become immune to the pain and suffering that so many people experienced during that armed campaign", he said. "To read the words written by an Irish band in such a compelling way was very, very powerful."[\[60\]](#cite_note-60)

### Criticism

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Criticism")\]

Paul Brannigan of *[Louder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Rock_\(magazine\) "Classic Rock (magazine)")* writes, "Not everyone, however, was impressed by \[O'Riordan's\] credentials for the role of commentator on one of the most complex conflicts of the modern era."[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") said it "trivialised" the events of the Troubles, and that the "heavy rock trudge" did not play to the band's strengths.[\[62\]](#cite_note-BogdanovWoodstra2002-62) [David Stubbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Stubbs "David Stubbs") from *[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker")* said, "'Zombie' doesn't make a born-again fan of me, with its lethargic, samey, grungy riff lurching predictably towards anthem status. But I like Dolores O' Riordan's vocal, like Dana on heroin, all tattered, snarling and trembling at her wits' end."[\[63\]](#cite_note-63) At the same time, Northern Irish band Schtum told *Melody Maker*, "She's from Limerick, what the fuck would she know? You're talking about the last 25 years of a much bigger and wider problem that has gone on for hundreds of years".[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61) Brannigan writes:

> Schtum hailed from Derry, a city 224 miles away from Limerick by road, but one which may as well have been on a different planet to the rural village where Dolores O’Riordan was raised. When the singer protested *"It's not me, it's not my family"*, explicitly distancing herself from the violence in Northern Ireland, and its overspill into England and elsewhere, she spoke the truth: no-one from her family was present at the [Battle of the Bogside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bogside "Battle of the Bogside") in Derry from August 12–14, 1969, for instance, or on January 30, 1972, when soldiers from the Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights campaigners in the city, killing 14 unarmed civilians in a massacre which came to be known as [Bloody Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Sunday_\(1972\) "Bloody Sunday (1972)"). Equally, her family had the good fortune to be untouched by any of the atrocities claimed by the Provisional IRA (or any other paramilitary faction) during her lifetime. So removed, in fact, was O’Riordan from events in Northern Ireland that, in her lyrics to Zombie, she references "tanks" on the streets, perhaps confusing Belfast with Beijing.[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61)

[Iestyn George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iestyn_George "Iestyn George") from *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Musical_Express "New Musical Express")* felt "the timing of this release, as much as the sentiment itself, seems more than a little askew".[\[64\]](#cite_note-64) Reviewing "Zombie" for *[Smash Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smash_Hits "Smash Hits")*, the pop-punk duo [Shampoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shampoo_\(duo\) "Shampoo (duo)") gave it two out of five.[\[65\]](#cite_note-65)

### Accolades

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Accolades")\]

On 23 November 1995, the Cranberries won the Best Song Award for "Zombie" at the [1995 MTV Europe Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MTV_Europe_Music_Awards "1995 MTV Europe Music Awards").[\[66\]](#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67) In November 2022, it was voted as the greatest Irish hit of all time by [RTÉ 2fm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTÉ_2fm "RTÉ 2fm") listeners in compiling the ultimate Irish playlist for a television special shown on [RTÉ One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTÉ_One "RTÉ One").[\[68\]](#cite_note-68)

### As a sporting anthem

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: As a sporting anthem")\]

Following the death of O'Riordan in 2018, the [hurling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurling "Hurling") team from her home county of [Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limerick_county_hurling_team "Limerick county hurling team") adopted "Zombie" as their anthem during their [successful run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_All-Ireland_Senior_Hurling_Championship_final "2018 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship final") to the [All-Ireland Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Ireland_Senior_Hurling_Championship "All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship"). It soon became a rugby anthem as well; Limerick-based [Munster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munster_Rugby "Munster Rugby") initially played it in tribute to O'Riordan, and crowd reaction led to it becoming a post-match staple.[\[69\]](#cite_note-69)

The song was re-popularised in 2023 after it was played after Ireland games at the [2023 Rugby World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Rugby_World_Cup "2023 Rugby World Cup"). It was picked up by fans of the Irish team, with videos of fans singing in chorus accumulating hundreds of thousands of views on social media.[\[70\]](#cite_note-:0-70) This offended Irish nationalists, who identified it as an "anti-IRA" anthem, and said that the lyrics failed to consider their experience during the Troubles.[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61)[\[71\]](#cite_note-71)

Irish political leaders supported the use of "Zombie" as a rugby anthem. [Taoiseach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoiseach "Taoiseach") [Leo Varadkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Varadkar "Leo Varadkar") described it as "a song that we can all sing comfortably. It’s an anti-terrorism song. It’s not a nationalist or unionist song." [SDLP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_and_Labour_Party "Social Democratic and Labour Party") leader [Colum Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colum_Eastwood "Colum Eastwood") wrote that "'Zombie' is an anti-war song written after the IRA killed 2 children in Warrington", adding that criticism of the IRA is not an endorsement of "British brutality", writing "Most of us opposed both".[\[70\]](#cite_note-:0-70)

The [Warrington Wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_Wolves "Warrington Wolves") rugby league team, who play in the [Super League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League "Super League"), began playing "Zombie" from the 2025 season onwards as a club anthem at every home match at the [Halliwell Jones Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halliwell_Jones_Stadium "Halliwell Jones Stadium"), with the club granted endorsement to use itby the family of Tim Parry. Prior to a home season fixture during May, a cover was performed by Warrington band The Ambersons, with Wolves fans in attendance encouraged to sing from the stands.[\[72\]](#cite_note-72)

"Zombie" was also the walkout music for [mixed martial artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_martial_arts "Mixed martial arts") [Jung Chan-sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Korean_Zombie "The Korean Zombie"), known as 'The Korean Zombie', throughout his time in the [Ultimate Fighting Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_Fighting_Championship "Ultimate Fighting Championship").[\[73\]](#cite_note-73)

[Aston Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_F.C. "Aston Villa F.C.") supporters have adopted a chant for [Johan Manzambi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Manzambi "Johan Manzambi"), based on "Zombie," replacing the original refrain with “In your head, in your head, Manzambi, Manzambi, bi, bi."[\[74\]](#cite_note-74)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

"Zombie" topped the charts in many countries.[\[16\]](#cite_note-UDM-Lawler20200919-16)[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67) On 29 October 1994, it went to No. 1 on the US *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* Alternative Airplay chart, spending twenty-three weeks on the chart.[\[75\]](#cite_note-75) In 1994, "Zombie" was "the most played song ever on alternative radio in the history of America", as mentioned in the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* and in Kenneth L. Campbell's book, *Ireland's History – Prehistory to the Present*.[\[32\]](#cite_note-LAT-Bream94-32)[\[76\]](#cite_note-76) [Junkee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junkee "Junkee") journalist Jules LeFevre recalled that Australian audiences were "particularly gripped by the song", with [Triple J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J "Triple J") listeners voting for "Zombie" as No. 1 on the [Triple J Hottest 100, 1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J_Hottest_100,_1994 "Triple J Hottest 100, 1994") chart,[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67)[\[77\]](#cite_note-77) establishing for the first time ever that a female vocalist won the [Triple J Hottest 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J_Hottest_100#Hottest_100_top_tens_and_summaries "Triple J Hottest 100").[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67) On 18 December 1994, it reached No. 1 on the [ARIA Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Charts "ARIA Charts"), where it remained for seven consecutive weeks.[\[78\]](#cite_note-78) The single peaked at No. 1 and spent twenty eight weeks on the [Official German Charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GfK_Entertainment_charts "GfK Entertainment charts").[\[79\]](#cite_note-79) On 25 December 1994, the single debuted at No. 27 on the [Ö3 Austria Top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ö3_Austria_Top_40 "Ö3 Austria Top 40"), and climbed to No. 2, where it stayed for eight weeks.[\[80\]](#cite_note-80) "Zombie" debuted on the [French SNEP Top 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_number-one_singles_of_1995_\(France\) "List of number-one singles of 1995 (France)") at No. 4 on 25 February 1995\. The following week, the single moved to No. 1; it spent nine consecutive weeks at the top and a total of forty-two weeks on the singles chart.[\[81\]](#cite_note-81) The song reached No. 14 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart").[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37)

"**Zombie**" is a [protest song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_song "Protest song") by Irish [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") band [the Cranberries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cranberries "The Cranberries"). It was written by the lead singer, [Dolores O'Riordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_O'Riordan "Dolores O'Riordan"), about the young victims of a [bombing in Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_bombings "Warrington bombings"), England, during [the Troubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles "The Troubles") in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland"). The song was released on 19 September 1994 by [Island Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Records "Island Records") as the [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single") from the Cranberries' second studio album, *[No Need to Argue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Need_to_Argue "No Need to Argue")* (1994). Critics have described "Zombie" as "a masterpiece of alternative rock", with [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge")\-style distorted guitar and shouted vocals uncharacteristic of the band's other work.

While Island Records feared releasing a politically charged song as a single, "Zombie" reached No. 1 on the charts of Australia, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, and Iceland. The song was ineligible for the US *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* [Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_100 "Hot 100") chart, but it reached No. 1 on the US *Billboard* [Alternative Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_Songs "Alternative Songs") chart. Listeners of the Australian radio station [Triple J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J "Triple J") voted it No. 1 on the [1994 Triple J Hottest 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J_Hottest_100,_1994 "Triple J Hottest 100, 1994") chart, and it won the Best Song Award at the [1995 MTV Europe Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MTV_Europe_Music_Awards "1995 MTV Europe Music Awards"). The music video was directed by [Samuel Bayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Bayer "Samuel Bayer"), and featured O'Riordan singing while painted gold, and footage of war-torn Belfast. In April 2020, it became the first song by an Irish group to surpass one billion views on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube").

The Cranberries noted that "Zombie" drew strong responses from audiences. After O'Riordan's death in 2018, it became an Irish [stadium anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium_anthem "Stadium anthem"), first for the teams from the Cranberries' hometown of [Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limerick "Limerick"), and later for the [Ireland national rugby union team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_national_rugby_union_team "Ireland national rugby union team") starting in the [2023 Rugby World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Rugby_World_Cup "2023 Rugby World Cup"). The band recorded acoustic, stripped-down versions on *[MTV Unplugged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Unplugged "MTV Unplugged")* and the 2017 album *[Something Else](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Something_Else_\(The_Cranberries_album\) "Something Else (The Cranberries album)")*. "Zombie" has been covered by numerous artists; O'Riordan had planned to contribute vocals to a version by the American band [Bad Wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Wolves "Bad Wolves"), which was released days after her death.

## Background and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and composition")\]

[The Troubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles "The Troubles") were a conflict in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") from the late 1960s to 1998\.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) The [Provisional Irish Republican Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army "Provisional Irish Republican Army") (IRA), an [Irish republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_republican "Irish republican") paramilitary organisation, waged an [armed campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army_campaign "Provisional Irish Republican Army campaign") to end British rule in Northern Ireland and [unite the region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Ireland "United Ireland") with the [Republic of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland"). Republican and [Loyalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_loyalism "Ulster loyalism") paramilitaries killed more than 3,500 people, many from [thousands of bomb attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bombings_during_the_Troubles "List of bombings during the Troubles").[\[4\]](#cite_note-Taulbee-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) One of the bombings happened on 20 March 1993, as two IRA [improvised explosive devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvised_explosive_device "Improvised explosive device") hidden in litter bins [were detonated in a shopping street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_bombings "Warrington bombings") in [Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington "Warrington"), England. Two children were killed in the attack: Johnathan Ball, aged 3, and Tim Parry, aged 12\. 56 people were injured.[\[6\]](#cite_note-UPI-1993-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Ball died at the scene of the bombing as a result of his fragmentation-inflicted injuries, and five days later, Parry died in a hospital as a result of head injuries.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) O'Riordan decided to write a song that reflected upon the event and the children's deaths after visiting the town:[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10)

> There were a lot of bombs going off in London and I remember this one time a child was killed when a bomb was put in a rubbish bin – that's why there's that line in the song, 'A child is slowly taken'. \[ ... \] We were on a tour bus and I was near the location where it happened, so it really struck me hard – I was quite young, but I remember being devastated about the innocent children being pulled into that kind of thing. So I suppose that's why I was saying, 'It's not me' – that even though I'm Irish it wasn't me, I didn't do it. Because being Irish, it was quite hard, especially in the UK when there was so much tension.

— Dolores O'Riordan in 2017, on writing "Zombie".[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10)

O'Riordan said "Zombie" came to her "subconsciously" midway through the Cranberries' English tour in 1993,[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) writing the core chords on her acoustic guitar.[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10) Once O'Riordan was back in her hometown of [Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limerick "Limerick") and returned to her flat after a night out,[\[12\]](#cite_note-LS-Johnston2017-12)[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10) she played those chords and started building a song around them, quickly "coming up with the chorus, which was catchy and anthemic",[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) and soon moving onto the verses.[\[10\]](#cite_note-SM-Linderman2019-10) O'Riordan took the song idea, originally titled "In Your Head", into the Cranberries' small rehearsal shed in [Mungret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mungret "Mungret").[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14) Given she was playing an acoustic guitar, the rest of the band initially followed along in, as guitarist [Noel Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Hogan "Noel Hogan") put it, "that kind of sweet [indie pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_pop "Indie pop") thing" that the band featured in their other songs, before O'Riordan decided that it was not what she wanted,[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15) picked up an electric guitar and stated that "it needs to be heavy because it's angry". Drummer Fergal Lawler recalled that usually in that small room, "you're trying to keep it low because you don't want to deafen anybody", but O'Riordan played it loud and "we couldn't really hear the lyrics because she was singing through her guitar", and that the singer was adamant that she wanted more [distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distortion_\(music\) "Distortion (music)") pedals on the guitars and asked for more strength than usual in drumming.[\[16\]](#cite_note-UDM-Lawler20200919-16)[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14)

## Production and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Production and release")\]

> "Years from now, when alternative rock is just a distant memory from a time long forgotten, certain songs will remain. 'Zombie' will forever live on as a true classic moment from a truly classic era of music. Not before or since has a band hit on a moment and absolutely capitalised like The Cranberries did with 'Zombie'. ... Thank you for giving us alternative rock's true masterpiece".

— Author Joe Hughes, in 2018\.[\[17\]](#cite_note-AN-Hughes2018-17)

Soon after "Zombie" was completed, the Cranberries added it to their set list. Lawler said they performed it for a year before recording it, and audiences responded with enthusiasm.[\[18\]](#cite_note-RS-Blistein2019-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) The song was recorded and mixed at [the Manor Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Manor_Studio "The Manor Studio") in Oxford\] and at [Townhouse Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townhouse_Studios "Townhouse Studios") in London in 1994 with producer [Stephen Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Street "Stephen Street").[\[20\]](#cite_note-studios-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-CDbooklet-21) They spent a long time working on getting the [guitar settings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_tunings "Guitar tunings") right to give a suitably expansive sound, with O'Riordan noting "the sound came organically, because we were using our live instruments, we were plugging in a lot, and we started to mess around with [feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_feedback "Audio feedback") and distortion".[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) Hogan contributed [rhythm guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_guitar "Rhythm guitar") to provide textures under O'Riordan's [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff").[\[22\]](#cite_note-Fuller2018-01-23-22) "Zombie" departed from the strings and [jangle guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jangle "Jangle") of the Cranberries' debut album, *[Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody_Else_Is_Doing_It,_So_Why_Can't_We%3F "Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?")* (1993).[\[12\]](#cite_note-LS-Johnston2017-12)[\[23\]](#cite_note-RS-Bienstock2018-23) Hogan said it made them realise "that you can actually be heavy and still have melody", marking a change in their composition style and performances.[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15)

Knowing its potential, the Cranberries wanted "Zombie" to be the lead single for their album *[No Need to Argue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Need_to_Argue "No Need to Argue")*.[\[18\]](#cite_note-RS-Blistein2019-18) Their former manager, Allen Kovac, said that [Island Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Records "Island Records") urged them not to release the "politically urgent" song as a single, and that O'Riordan had ripped up a $1-million cheque the label offered her to work on another song.[\[24\]](#cite_note-RS-Browne2018-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOM-2020-01-15-25) "Dolores was a very small, fragile person, but very opinionated," said Kovac. "Her belief was that she was an international artist and she wanted to break the rest of the world, and 'Zombie' was part of that evolution. She felt the need to expand beyond 'I love you, you love me' and write about what was happening in Ireland at the time", he said.[\[24\]](#cite_note-RS-Browne2018-24) Island Records and management also said "Zombie" was "too controversial, you might not get played on the radio".[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) Hogan added that the label were not expecting a lead single sounding different from the band's output "instead of coming out with another '[Linger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linger_\(The_Cranberries_song\) "Linger (The Cranberries song)")' or '[Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreams_\(The_Cranberries_song\) "Dreams (The Cranberries song)")'".[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15) Lawler recalled arguing to the record label that during the year the band had played "Zombie" in concert, "for a new song that the audience hadn't heard before, they really reacted to it",[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) which was "a sign that it's a catchy song. People like it. It has to work.”[\[15\]](#cite_note-forbes-15) Over time, "\[w\]e pushed and pushed and eventually they decided to release it", he said.[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) By the time the single for "Zombie" was released on 19 September 1994,[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) as well as its parent album *No Need to Argue* the following month, with a music video in heavy rotation on [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV"), the Cranberries were catapulted to international stardom.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](#cite_note-NYT-20180116-28) Shortly after, ideological beliefs came rushing to the forefront of local newspapers, criticising O'Riordan for writing about the Troubles.[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14) O'Riordan said she "knew that would be the angle of the song, because it was controversial".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) Assessing the cultural impact of their song, Hogan responded: "Because of this song, people thought we were a political band. ... Far from it. Dolores always wrote from the heart".[\[14\]](#cite_note-TIME-Barter2019-14) O'Riordan would later state, "If I think something, I have to say it. And I really don't care what anybody thinks, you know?".[\[30\]](#cite_note-NPR-Limbong2018-30) *[NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR")*'s Andrew Limbong, speaking after O'Riordan's death in 2018, said "even though it was a political song, it wasn't necessarily politics she was interested in writing about".[\[30\]](#cite_note-NPR-Limbong2018-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-VOX1994-31) O'Riordan said, "I just cannot accept children being slaughtered at the hands of political violence", and hoped that "it might make people reflect a bit on our society and what we've become."[\[32\]](#cite_note-LAT-Bream94-32)

## Music and lyrics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music and lyrics")\]

"Zombie" has been characterised by commentators as [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock")[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) and [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge").[\[35\]](#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](#cite_note-36) O'Riordan later said it was not a concerted effort to ride the grunge movement, but she stated that "this wasn't grunge, but the timing was good", adding that, "We were just a different type of a band... and we had a lot of our own ideas".[\[12\]](#cite_note-LS-Johnston2017-12)[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) Hogan noted in a *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* interview that the Cranberries were beforehand accepted by "the same kind of \[grunge\] audience".[\[23\]](#cite_note-RS-Bienstock2018-23) O'Riordan was responsible for the heavier sound,[\[19\]](#cite_note-Conner-2020-11-13-19) a mere expression of her musical taste, as she would say later "we got it out of our system... all that anger out of our system".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) Discussing the musical approach and the requirement of a sound significantly louder, Hogan explained in a 2012 interview with [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam")'s *FaceCulture* that "the heavier sound was the right thing for the song. If it was soft, it wouldn't have had that impact. It would stand out in the live set because of that."[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) Particularly offended that [terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army#Categorisation "Provisional Irish Republican Army") claimed to have carried out these acts in the name of Ireland,[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) O'Riordan asserted: "The IRA are not me. I'm not the IRA. The Cranberries are not the IRA. My family are not. When it says in the song, '*It's not me, it's not my family*,' that's what I'm saying. It's not Ireland, it's some idiots living in the past."[\[31\]](#cite_note-VOX1994-31)[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37) O'Riordan received criticism for the "hard-hitting lyrics"; she responded that it was written from a humanitarian perspective.[\[13\]](#cite_note-UDM-20200418-13) O’Riordan's mother, Eileen, said: "It wasn’t written as a political song but as an anti-violence, an anti-war song."[\[38\]](#cite_note-38)

O'Riordan never revealed the origin of the "zombie" reference in the lyrics, a concept which admits a personal interpretation of its meaning.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) However, there was a divergence of opinion among writers on the subject. Writing for *The Telegraph*, Ed Power formulated his own hypothesis, saying that the word *Zombie* was "a commentary on how blindly cleaving to centuries old prejudices can reduce \[one's\] capacity for independent thought".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-Power-29) *Culture Trip* writer Graham Fuller commented that the metaphor perhaps "reanimates the children whose deaths inspired O'Riordan to write it".[\[22\]](#cite_note-Fuller2018-01-23-22) Sonia Saraiya, music and TV critic from *[Miami Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Herald "Miami Herald")* and *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")*, had a different view, saying that the *Zombie* is not the dead children, but "the dead children that populate your mind; the dead bodies you've seen in the images that you can't forget".[\[39\]](#cite_note-VARIETY-Saraiya2018-39)

### Singing voice

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Singing voice")\]

O'Riordan's vocals were noted as reminiscent of the [sean-nós singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean-nós_singing "Sean-nós singing") style,[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41)[\[28\]](#cite_note-NYT-20180116-28) for the [rapid and repeated changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato "Vibrato") in [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_\(music\) "Pitch (music)"), most notably [yodeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yodeling "Yodeling")[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41) when she does the sharp break[\[42\]](#cite_note-42) from [chest register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chest_register "Chest register") to [head register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_register "Head register") in the second [syllable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable "Syllable") of the word *Zom-bie*,[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41) and doing an [amplified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_resonation "Vocal resonation") method forming her [vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowels "Vowels") and [consonants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonants "Consonants").[\[41\]](#cite_note-TNR-Livingstone-41) This creates a vocal trademark when combined with the Gaelic [keening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keening "Keening"),[\[43\]](#cite_note-43) the [lilting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilting "Lilting") vocables,[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) and sung in her thick [Irish accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brogue_\(accent\) "Brogue (accent)").[\[45\]](#cite_note-TIME-20180116-45)[\[28\]](#cite_note-NYT-20180116-28) Author [Bart Plantenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bart_Plantenga "Bart Plantenga") wrote in his book *Yodel in Hi-Fi: From Kitsch Folk to Contemporary Electronica* that "\[h\]er waify, quavering, breaking voice has a natural 'Celtic yodel' in it. It can also be heard on 'Zombie'" \[and other songs\] used "for fantastic emotional effect".[\[46\]](#cite_note-46) Mikael Wood of *Los Angeles Times* described O'Riordan "pushing her voice to a jagged extreme to embody the pain", with a "desperate, yodeling vocal that conjures some ancient emotion".[\[47\]](#cite_note-47) *Far Out Magazine* commented that her vocal performance was "guttural, pleading, captivating and utterly unique, O'Riordan begs for humanity the only way she knew how".[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOM-2020-01-15-25) Saraiya wrote that her voice "often seemed bigger than her petite frame", and also commented that the chorus "practically grunted out of her otherwise bell-like voice with a guttural vowel sound".[\[39\]](#cite_note-VARIETY-Saraiya2018-39)

> O'Riordan's voice is just in a league all its own. She makes no effort to hide her accent. In fact, it adds a richness and character to her voice. O'Riordan lays it all out on the table. Beautifully. Uncompromising and unrelenting. O'Riordan sinks her hooks into you and holds you hostage with her breathtaking vocal onslaught.

— Joe Hughes, *How The Cranberries Blew Away Nirvana With Definitive Grunge Song "Zombie"* – *Alternative Nation*.[\[17\]](#cite_note-AN-Hughes2018-17)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

### Praise

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Praise")\]

*Tedium'*s editor, Ernie Smith, said that O'Riordan wrote "Zombie" in a moment of anger and passion, and called it "one of the defining songs of the alternative rock era".[\[48\]](#cite_note-TEDIUM-48) Rebecca Black of the *[Belfast Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast_Telegraph "Belfast Telegraph")* described "Zombie" as an "outraged response to the Warrington bombs",[\[49\]](#cite_note-49) while music reporter Mark Savage wrote that "her pain was real", describing it as "a visceral response to the death of two children".[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37) In a contemporary review, *[Hot Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Press "Hot Press")* praised "Zombie" and its arrangements, saying that it was stylistically different from the band's previous works: "[Staccato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staccato "Staccato") rhythms and subtle jerks and pauses in the music and the singing make this more than just business-as-usual for the Cranberries. A slow, brooding [Siouxsie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siouxsie_Sioux "Siouxsie Sioux")\-like buzzing guitar melody and dirge-like bass and drums counterpoint the elliptical and impassioned vocals of Dolores O'Riordan as she works her way through the internal psychic and external human tragedies of the Troubles \[...\] "Zombie" signals a growth in confidence".[\[50\]](#cite_note-50) *[The Rough Guide to Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_Guides#Music "Rough Guides")* identified the album *No Need to Argue* as "more of the same" as the Cranberries' debut album, except for the song "Zombie", which had an "angry grunge" sound and "aggressive" lyrics.[\[51\]](#cite_note-51) Music critic [Evelyn McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_McDonnell "Evelyn McDonnell") allowed that O'Riordan had a "certain naivety to her and also a real toughness".[\[30\]](#cite_note-NPR-Limbong2018-30) New York arts editor Graham Fuller partially echoed this view, saying "she was right, but that naivety serves a song that's an unfiltered reaction to a tragedy. It goes with Zombie's primal fury; slicker lyrics would have diluted the song's rawness."[\[22\]](#cite_note-Fuller2018-01-23-22)

Music critic [Neil McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_McCormick "Neil McCormick") wrote that it was the Cranberries' "fiercest rock song... An accusatory lament, it grapples with the endless recriminations of the Irish Troubles, with a slow rolling bass line and thumping mid-tempo beat, finding tension between melodic delicacy and introspection in the verses with a keening, wailing chorus charged with distorted grungy guitars".[\[52\]](#cite_note-52) *[Music & Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_&_Media "Music & Media")* stated that it "combines moody soundscapes with some grunge-y guitar attacks that together make an arresting number".[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) Mark Morris from *[Select](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Select_\(magazine\) "Select (magazine)")* wrote in his review of the album, "The surprise is 'Zombie', a [Sinéad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinéad_O'Connor "Sinéad O'Connor")\-like tantrum of crunchy guitars and confused lyrics about guns and bombs."[\[54\]](#cite_note-54) [Charles Aaron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Aaron "Charles Aaron") from *[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_\(magazine\) "Spin (magazine)")* commented, "I like "Zombie" because its crunching, troubled guitar fuzz was the loudest thing on MTV during the last days of '94. Just ask Bono, my Irish Setter. He's still wailing."[\[55\]](#cite_note-55) Josh Jones of Open Culture, described the "[Gen X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_X#Arts_and_culture "Generation X") heyday"'s song, as "O'Riordan's stadium-size hit ... and its beautifully pained laments and pointedly unsubtle yelps and wails—a stunning expression of mourning that reverberates still some 25 years later".[\[56\]](#cite_note-OC-Jones2018-56) Martin Aston of *[Music Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Week "Music Week")* wrote: "Having broken the UK on the back of their US success, the Cranberries continue to use their pop acumen to fashion wonderful, wistful pop nuggets. 'Zombie' is a little heavier and less user-friendly than 'Linger' and 'Dreams', but no less sublime for it."[\[57\]](#cite_note-57) In 2018, *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* and *[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")* ranked it number three and number two, respectively, on their lists of the top ten Cranberries songs.[\[58\]](#cite_note-58)[\[59\]](#cite_note-59)

On 16 January 2018, following O'Riordan's death, [Colin Parry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tim_Parry_Johnathan_Ball_Foundation_for_Peace "The Tim Parry Johnathan Ball Foundation for Peace"), father of IRA victim Tim Parry, thanked O'Riordan for the "both majestic and also very real lyrics".[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37) "Many people have become immune to the pain and suffering that so many people experienced during that armed campaign", he said. "To read the words written by an Irish band in such a compelling way was very, very powerful."[\[60\]](#cite_note-60)

### Criticism

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Criticism")\]

Paul Brannigan of *[Louder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Rock_\(magazine\) "Classic Rock (magazine)")* writes, "Not everyone, however, was impressed by \[O'Riordan's\] credentials for the role of commentator on one of the most complex conflicts of the modern era."[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") said it "trivialised" the events of the Troubles, and that the "heavy rock trudge" did not play to the band's strengths.[\[62\]](#cite_note-BogdanovWoodstra2002-62) [David Stubbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Stubbs "David Stubbs") from *[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker")* said, "'Zombie' doesn't make a born-again fan of me, with its lethargic, samey, grungy riff lurching predictably towards anthem status. But I like Dolores O' Riordan's vocal, like Dana on heroin, all tattered, snarling and trembling at her wits' end."[\[63\]](#cite_note-63) At the same time, Northern Irish band Schtum told *Melody Maker*, "She's from Limerick, what the fuck would she know? You're talking about the last 25 years of a much bigger and wider problem that has gone on for hundreds of years".[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61) Brannigan writes:

> Schtum hailed from Derry, a city 224 miles away from Limerick by road, but one which may as well have been on a different planet to the rural village where Dolores O’Riordan was raised. When the singer protested *"It's not me, it's not my family"*, explicitly distancing herself from the violence in Northern Ireland, and its overspill into England and elsewhere, she spoke the truth: no-one from her family was present at the [Battle of the Bogside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bogside "Battle of the Bogside") in Derry from August 12–14, 1969, for instance, or on January 30, 1972, when soldiers from the Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights campaigners in the city, killing 14 unarmed civilians in a massacre which came to be known as [Bloody Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Sunday_\(1972\) "Bloody Sunday (1972)"). Equally, her family had the good fortune to be untouched by any of the atrocities claimed by the Provisional IRA (or any other paramilitary faction) during her lifetime. So removed, in fact, was O’Riordan from events in Northern Ireland that, in her lyrics to Zombie, she references "tanks" on the streets, perhaps confusing Belfast with Beijing.[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61)

[Iestyn George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iestyn_George "Iestyn George") from *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Musical_Express "New Musical Express")* felt "the timing of this release, as much as the sentiment itself, seems more than a little askew".[\[64\]](#cite_note-64) Reviewing "Zombie" for *[Smash Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smash_Hits "Smash Hits")*, the pop-punk duo [Shampoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shampoo_\(duo\) "Shampoo (duo)") gave it two out of five.[\[65\]](#cite_note-65)

### Accolades

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Accolades")\]

On 23 November 1995, the Cranberries won the Best Song Award for "Zombie" at the [1995 MTV Europe Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MTV_Europe_Music_Awards "1995 MTV Europe Music Awards").[\[66\]](#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67) In November 2022, it was voted as the greatest Irish hit of all time by [RTÉ 2fm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTÉ_2fm "RTÉ 2fm") listeners in compiling the ultimate Irish playlist for a television special shown on [RTÉ One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTÉ_One "RTÉ One").[\[68\]](#cite_note-68)

### As a sporting anthem

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Zombie_\(The_Cranberries_song\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: As a sporting anthem")\]

Following the death of O'Riordan in 2018, the [hurling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurling "Hurling") team from her home county of [Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limerick_county_hurling_team "Limerick county hurling team") adopted "Zombie" as their anthem during their [successful run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_All-Ireland_Senior_Hurling_Championship_final "2018 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship final") to the [All-Ireland Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Ireland_Senior_Hurling_Championship "All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship"). It soon became a rugby anthem as well; Limerick-based [Munster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munster_Rugby "Munster Rugby") initially played it in tribute to O'Riordan, and crowd reaction led to it becoming a post-match staple.[\[69\]](#cite_note-69)

The song was re-popularised in 2023 after it was played after Ireland games at the [2023 Rugby World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Rugby_World_Cup "2023 Rugby World Cup"). It was picked up by fans of the Irish team, with videos of fans singing in chorus accumulating hundreds of thousands of views on social media.[\[70\]](#cite_note-:0-70) This offended Irish nationalists, who identified it as an "anti-IRA" anthem, and said that the lyrics failed to consider their experience during the Troubles.[\[61\]](#cite_note-Louder-61)[\[71\]](#cite_note-71)

Irish political leaders supported the use of "Zombie" as a rugby anthem. [Taoiseach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoiseach "Taoiseach") [Leo Varadkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Varadkar "Leo Varadkar") described it as "a song that we can all sing comfortably. It’s an anti-terrorism song. It’s not a nationalist or unionist song." [SDLP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_and_Labour_Party "Social Democratic and Labour Party") leader [Colum Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colum_Eastwood "Colum Eastwood") wrote that "'Zombie' is an anti-war song written after the IRA killed 2 children in Warrington", adding that criticism of the IRA is not an endorsement of "British brutality", writing "Most of us opposed both".[\[70\]](#cite_note-:0-70)

The [Warrington Wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_Wolves "Warrington Wolves") rugby league team, who play in the [Super League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League "Super League"), began playing "Zombie" from the 2025 season onwards as a club anthem at every home match at the [Halliwell Jones Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halliwell_Jones_Stadium "Halliwell Jones Stadium"), with the club granted endorsement to use itby the family of Tim Parry. Prior to a home season fixture during May, a cover was performed by Warrington band The Ambersons, with Wolves fans in attendance encouraged to sing from the stands.[\[72\]](#cite_note-72)

"Zombie" was also the walkout music for [mixed martial artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_martial_arts "Mixed martial arts") [Jung Chan-sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Korean_Zombie "The Korean Zombie"), known as 'The Korean Zombie', throughout his time in the [Ultimate Fighting Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_Fighting_Championship "Ultimate Fighting Championship").[\[73\]](#cite_note-73)

[Aston Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_F.C. "Aston Villa F.C.") supporters have adopted a chant for [Johan Manzambi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Manzambi "Johan Manzambi"), based on "Zombie," replacing the original refrain with “In your head, in your head, Manzambi, Manzambi, bi, bi."[\[74\]](#cite_note-74)

"Zombie" topped the charts in many countries.[\[16\]](#cite_note-UDM-Lawler20200919-16)[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67) On 29 October 1994, it went to No. 1 on the US *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* Alternative Airplay chart, spending twenty-three weeks on the chart.[\[75\]](#cite_note-75) In 1994, "Zombie" was "the most played song ever on alternative radio in the history of America", as mentioned in the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* and in Kenneth L. Campbell's book, *Ireland's History – Prehistory to the Present*.[\[32\]](#cite_note-LAT-Bream94-32)[\[76\]](#cite_note-76) [Junkee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junkee "Junkee") journalist Jules LeFevre recalled that Australian audiences were "particularly gripped by the song", with [Triple J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J "Triple J") listeners voting for "Zombie" as No. 1 on the [Triple J Hottest 100, 1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J_Hottest_100,_1994 "Triple J Hottest 100, 1994") chart,[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67)[\[77\]](#cite_note-77) establishing for the first time ever that a female vocalist won the [Triple J Hottest 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_J_Hottest_100#Hottest_100_top_tens_and_summaries "Triple J Hottest 100").[\[67\]](#cite_note-Junkee-TJH100-67) On 18 December 1994, it reached No. 1 on the [ARIA Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Charts "ARIA Charts"), where it remained for seven consecutive weeks.[\[78\]](#cite_note-78) The single peaked at No. 1 and spent twenty eight weeks on the [Official German Charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GfK_Entertainment_charts "GfK Entertainment charts").[\[79\]](#cite_note-79) On 25 December 1994, the single debuted at No. 27 on the [Ö3 Austria Top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ö3_Austria_Top_40 "Ö3 Austria Top 40"), and climbed to No. 2, where it stayed for eight weeks.[\[80\]](#cite_note-80) "Zombie" debuted on the [French SNEP Top 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_number-one_singles_of_1995_\(France\) "List of number-one singles of 1995 (France)") at No. 4 on 25 February 1995\. The following week, the single moved to No. 1; it spent nine consecutive weeks at the top and a total of forty-two weeks on the singles chart.[\[81\]](#cite_note-81) The song reached No. 14 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart").[\[37\]](#cite_note-BBC2016-37)
